unit-m5u7.title: Unit 5 · Lesson 7: Use Different Strategies to Divide
unit-m5u7.source: enVision Topic 5 Student Edition practice pages — dividing by two-digit divisors (Drive)

summary.text: Lesson 5-7 practice pages: choosing a strategy to divide (estimating, patterns, partial quotients and long division), checking that a quotient is reasonable, deciding whether a remainder can be bigger than the divisor, and two-step word problems.

why.text: This lesson ties the unit together: the point is knowing which tool fits a problem, not just how to use each one.

objectives.text: Choose a strategy that fits the numbers in a division
Estimate a quotient and use it to check for reasonableness
Explain why a remainder must be smaller than the divisor
Divide four-digit numbers by two-digit divisors
Solve two-step word problems that use division

parentNote.text: Built from the lesson 5-7 practice pages in her Unit 5 folder, read for what they ask. The numbers are fresh, not the page's own. The slip most worth a word is a lost zero: 4,560 ÷ 19 is 240, and an estimate of 4,600 ÷ 20 = 230 catches an answer of 24 before she multiplies. Every wrong option on a worked division comes from a named slip (a partial quotient left out, a zero lost or added, the remainder left off, or a remainder bigger than the divisor). There was no lesson 5-6 page in the folder, so nothing was built for Lesson 6.

nextUp.text: Estimate, choose a strategy, divide, then check against the estimate.

cards.def:
**Before you divide, find two numbers the quotient sits between.**
• 2,890 ÷ 17: 17 × 100 = 1,700 and 17 × 200 = 3,400, so between 100 and 200.

**When both numbers end in zeros, use a basic fact and count the zeros.**
• 5,600 ÷ 80: 56 ÷ 8 = 7, so 70.

**For a big dividend, take away hundreds of groups first, then tens, then ones.**
• 9,216 ÷ 48: 100, then 90, then 2, for 192.

**Divide, multiply, subtract, bring down, one digit at a time.**
• Write 0 when a brought-down number is too small: 6,147 ÷ 61 = 100 R47.
cards.hint: Every brought-down digit gets a digit in the quotient.

cards.def:
**Pick the strategy that fits the numbers.**
• Zeros on both numbers: patterns.
• Messy numbers: partial quotients or long division.
• "About how many": an estimate is enough.

**A remainder is always smaller than the divisor.**
• 1,250 ÷ 32 is 39 R2, not 38 R34.
cards.hint: If another group fits, keep going.

cards.def:
**Compare your answer with your estimate. If it is about ten times too big or too small, a zero slipped.**
• 4,560 ÷ 19 is about 230, so 24 cannot be right.

**In a word problem, the quotient is often only the first step.**
• 2,880 eggs ÷ 12 = 240 cartons, then 240 × $3 = $720.
cards.hint: Ask what the question wants at the very end.

questions.q: Can a remainder be greater than the divisor?
opts: No, because then at least one more group would fit
Yes, whenever the dividend is very large
Yes, a remainder can be any number at all
No, because a remainder must always be zero
questions.hint: If 30 are left and the divisor is 24, what could you still do?
steps: A remainder is what is left when no more full groups fit.
If it were as big as the divisor, one more group would fit.
So the remainder is always smaller than the divisor.

ex.main: **No.** If what is left is as big as the divisor, another group fits, so you are not finished.
ex.tip: A remainder of 0 is fine; a remainder bigger than the divisor is not.

questions.q: The quotient of 2,890 ÷ 17 is between which two numbers?
steps: So the quotient is between 100 and 200.

ex.main: **100 and 200.** 17 × 100 = 1,700 and 17 × 200 = 3,400, and 2,890 is between them. The quotient is 170.
ex.tip: Multiplying by 10, 100 and 1,000 brackets the answer fast.

opts: Adding 80 over and over until the total reaches 5,600
Partial quotients, taking away one group of 80 at a time
A basic fact and patterns: 56 ÷ 8 = 7, so the answer is 70
questions.hint: Both numbers end in zero. Which lesson used that?
steps: 5,600 has two zeros and 80 has one, so one zero is left.

ex.main: **A basic fact and patterns.** 56 ÷ 8 = 7, and one zero is left over, so 70. The other ways work too, but take much longer.
ex.tip: Pick the strategy that fits the numbers.

questions.q: How many digits will the quotient of 4,176 ÷ 36 have?
steps: So the quotient is in the hundreds: three digits.

ex.main: **Three digits.** 36 × 100 = 3,600 fits under 4,176, but 36 × 1,000 does not, so the answer is in the hundreds: 116.
ex.tip: Knowing the number of digits first catches a lost or extra zero.

ex.main: **136.** Check: 24 × 136 = 3,264. The wrong answers come from real slips: 36 is a partial quotient left out of the sum; 135 R24 is one group short, which leaves a remainder too big to keep; 137 is one group too many.
ex.tip: Estimate: 3,000 ÷ 20 = 150, so expect a three-digit answer.

ex.main: **155.** Check: 38 × 155 = 5,890. The wrong answers come from real slips: 55 is a partial quotient left out of the sum; 1,550 is a zero too many; 156 is one group too many.

steps: 15 is less than 42, so 15 is the remainder.

ex.main: **175 R15.** Check: 42 × 175 + 15 = 7,365. The wrong answers come from real slips: 175 is the remainder left off; 174 R57 is one group short, which leaves a remainder too big to keep; 75 R15 is a partial quotient left out of the sum.
ex.tip: The remainder must be smaller than 42.

questions.hint: 61 fits into 61 once. What about the 4 that comes next?
steps: 61 does not fit into 6, so start with 61.
61 ÷ 61 is 1: 1 × 61 = 61, and 61 − 61 = 0. Bring down the 4 to make 4.
4 is less than 61, so write 0 in the quotient. Bring down the 7 to make 47.
47 is less than 61, so write 0 in the quotient.

ex.main: **100 R47.** Check: 61 × 100 + 47 = 6,147. The wrong answers come from real slips: 10 R47 is the zero in the quotient skipped; 100 is the remainder left off; 99 R108 is one group short, which leaves a remainder too big to keep.
ex.tip: A zero in the quotient holds a place.

questions.q: A stadium has 9,216 seats in sections of 48 seats each. How many sections are there?
questions.hint: Estimate first: 48 is close to 50. Then take away 48 × 100.

ex.main: **192 sections.** 48 × 192 = 9,216. 92 leaves the 100 out, 193 is one group too many, and 1,920 has a zero too many.

questions.q: Which division has a quotient of 64?

ex.main: **2,752 ÷ 43.** 43 × 64 = 2,752. The others are one group more, one group fewer, and ten times as much.
ex.tip: To find a dividend, multiply the divisor by the quotient.

questions.q: A farm packs 2,880 eggs into cartons of 12 and sells each carton for $3. How much money does it make if it sells every carton?
questions.hint: First find the number of cartons. Then find the money.

ex.main: **$720.** 2,880 ÷ 12 = 240 cartons, and 240 × $3 = $720. $240 stops after the first step, $8,640 multiplies the eggs instead of the cartons, and $72 loses a zero.
ex.tip: The price is per carton, so you need the cartons first.

questions.q: Ana says 4,560 ÷ 19 = 24. Which estimate shows her answer is not reasonable?
opts: 4,560 − 19 = 4,541, so an answer of 24 must be right
4,600 ÷ 20 is about 23, so 24 is close enough to be right
45 ÷ 19 is about 2, so 24 is about the right size
4,600 ÷ 20 = 230, so the answer should be in the hundreds
questions.hint: Round 19 to 20 and 4,560 to a number 20 divides easily.
steps: 4,560 is close to 4,600, and 19 is close to 20.
24 is about ten times too small.

ex.main: **4,600 ÷ 20 = 230, so the answer is in the hundreds.** The real quotient is 240. She lost a zero.
ex.tip: An estimate catches a missing zero before you multiply.

questions.q: Ben found 1,250 ÷ 32 = 38 R34. What should he fix?
opts: 34 is more than 32, so one more group fits: 39 R2
He should drop the remainder and write 38
He should write the remainder as a digit: 3,834
questions.hint: Compare the remainder with the divisor.
steps: 34 is more than 32, so another group fits.

ex.main: **One more group fits: 39 R2.** His check adds up, but a remainder must be smaller than the divisor.
ex.tip: A remainder bigger than the divisor means one digit is too small.

questions.q: A museum guide leads tours of exactly 26 people. One month, 6,422 people took a tour, and every tour was full. How many tours ran?

ex.main: **247 tours.** 26 × 247 = 6,422. 47 leaves out the 200, 248 is one too many, and 246 stops one group short.
ex.tip: Every tour was full, so the division comes out with nothing left.

questions.q: A school needs at least 1,000 pencils. Pencils come in boxes of 24. How many boxes should it order?

ex.main: **42 boxes.** 41 boxes hold 984 pencils, 16 short of 1,000, so the school needs one more box. 16 is the remainder, and "41 R16 boxes" cannot be ordered.
ex.tip: When you need at least a certain amount, round up.
